indicators.note: something upset has been knocked over and left in disarray, and letters in disarray are letters no longer standing in their proper order.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder, the two words taken together

explanation.surface: The man running the hotel has annoyed a visiting choir leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hotel' is the word a solver reaches for first as the NATO letter H, and it is plain fodder. The man wanted is the English choir trainer who built amateur choirs on television and took a military wives' choir to a Christmas number one.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: he trains and conducts choirs for a living, so he is one particular choirmaster rather than the word's general sense.

indicators.note: 'Short' asks for a curtailed version of the word beside it, so the tail of that word is left off and only its front survives.

parts.note: an old-fashioned girl's name; crossword 'girl' clues never say which girl, and any name of the right shape will do

explanation.surface: A girl of no great height, and happy enough about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letters go, and nothing in the clue says how many — you find the cut by working back from the length. The little word 'is' is joinery and belongs to neither half.
explanation.definitionFit: Glad and pleased are the same plain adjective for being happy about something: either one fills 'I'm ___ you came'.

clue.text: Transport rickety trap by the river

indicators.note: something rickety is loosely put together and ready to fall apart, so its letters will not hold the order they arrived in.

parts.note: the four letters of 'trap' in a different order
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire, and its three letters make it a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A wobbly pony-trap standing at the waterside, waiting to take somebody somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' reads as the ride the trap would give you and is wanted in its other sense, the one that survives in a transport of delight. A trap is a light two-wheeled carriage, which is what holds the picture together.
explanation.definitionFit: Transport as a noun means being carried out of yourself by feeling, a sense that now lives almost entirely in that one phrase.

indicators.note: 'First in' names the opening position of the word that follows, so only the letter standing at the front of it is wanted.

parts.note: the letter at the front of 'theatre'
an outbreak of spots on the skin is a rash

explanation.surface: The first person through the theatre doors notices rubbish left on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' looks like the verb holding the sentence up and is really a noun. Reading straight through as one continuous remark is what keeps the seam between the two pieces out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Litter is rubbish dropped where it should not be, and the answer is the everyday American noun for rubbish of any kind.

clue.text: Amid glib feud, centres of environment

indicators.note: 'centres of' asks for what sits at the heart of each word named, so the outer letters fall away and the middle stays.

parts.note: the middle two letters of a four-letter word
the same again, the pair either side of the centre line
and the middle pair of the third word

explanation.surface: A smooth-talking quarrel going on right in the middle of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction sits after its fodder and points backwards, so 'environment' looks like the word being gutted when it is really the definition. All three fodder words are four letters, which is what makes each centre a clean pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A milieu is the social surroundings a person moves in, which is what environment means once it is people rather than air and water.

indicators.note: 'twice' says the instruction in front of it is to be carried out a second time, so two answers to the same word stand end to end.

parts.note: to observe a thing is to look at it
the same word answered a second way, since to observe is also to see

explanation.surface: An instruction to give something a second inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves mean the same thing, so the clue names one instruction and counts it twice. The 4-3 enumeration is the only warning that two words are coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A once-over is a quick inspection given to something, and the answer is that same casual glance under a more informal name.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the pleasant word goes round the picked letter

parts.note: nice means pleasant, agreeable

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter of the word is used

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A family member says nice things about her mother's brother.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of uncle ('finally') sits inside NICE, which goes 'about' it. The clue's uncle is a red herring for the relation, though apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of one's brother or sister, so she is a family relation.

definitions.meaning: a small inflamed swelling on the eyelid, and the plainest description of one is a soreness of the eye
anything ugly enough that you would rather not be looking at it — a gasworks at the end of a pretty street

explanation.surface: A flat medical observation that a stye is unpleasant to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing marks the join, because the clue is a grammatical sentence from end to end and 'is' does duty as both verb and hinge. The gap between the two halves is a space that the answer does not have.
explanation.definitionFit: Run together, the word means anything ugly to look at; taken as its two halves, it is a sore on the eye, which is exactly what a stye is.

indicators.note: 'from' asks for something taken out of what follows rather than built up beside it, and what comes out of words is a run of their letters.

parts.note: five letters in a row, beginning partway through the first word and stopping partway through the second

explanation.surface: A note delivered by a genuine ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' sends most solvers hunting for an abbreviation or a piece of post; the Greek alphabet is the sense wanted. The run starts in the middle of a word, which is where the eye never looks.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, so the bare word 'letter' names what it is without any stretching.

indicators.note: to interpret a piece of music is to play it your own way rather than as written, and letters played that way come out in an order of their own.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the place and the performance run together

explanation.surface: A recital given alone in Ely, played freely rather than by the book.
explanation.walkthrough: Ely is the small cathedral city in the Cambridgeshire fens, and its three letters are here to supply fodder and nothing else. The indicator sits where a solver expects the definition to begin.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosely means without precision — a rule loosely applied is applied vaguely — and both are adverbs of the same shape.

indicators.note: to masquerade is to go about dressed as something you are not, and letters in disguise are letters not wearing their own order.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder, both words taken whole

explanation.surface: A reader objecting to sentimental mush being passed off as hard-edged writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slush' carries its sentimental sense here, which is what lets the surface argue about books rather than weather. The indicator is buried mid-clue where it reads as an ordinary verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruthlessness is the quality of showing no pity, which is what brutality names — both abstract nouns for treating people hard.

indicators.note: 'about' here means scattered around rather than wrapped round, so the letters are lying loose and may be picked up in any order.

parts.note: the article handed over as the letter it is
a grown-up is an adult
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Flattering a mature person on the subject of their vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the standard word for putting one piece round another, and there is nothing here for it to wrap. Seven letters arriving in three unequal pieces is an unusual shape for an anagram, and part of why it hides.
explanation.definitionFit: To adulate is to praise somebody fulsomely, so the plain verb substitutes for it directly, minus the excess.

clue.text: Boring and dull carrying bit of corn

indicators.note: a thing that carries another has it aboard and inside it, so one word here is holding the other within its letters.

parts.note: a dull lecture is a dry one
corn grows in ears, so one bit of it is an ear

explanation.surface: Something tedious and humourless going about with a single corncob aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring and dull' reads as one doubled-up description, which hides the fact that only the first word is the definition. 'Bit of' usually asks for a single letter and here wants a whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary and boring both describe something that goes on without interest or variety, and either adjective fits 'a ___ afternoon'.

parts.note: the thing you shake over a pram
R is the standard short form of right

explanation.surface: A child's toy lying on the ground next to a snake.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay point at the same noise, which is what makes the join invisible. R for right is the abbreviation from maps and stage directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattler is the everyday American name for a rattlesnake, taken from the horny rings it shakes as a warning.

definitions.note: 'One laments' stands in for 'one who laments': the setter drops the relative pronoun, which is the usual way a cryptic clue defines an agent noun.
definitions.meaning: to keen is to wail aloud in grief, a formal part of Irish and Scottish funerals, and the person hired to do it takes a name from the verb
the ordinary comparative of keen, as in a sharper appetite or a fiercer wind

explanation.surface: Somebody regretting that matters have grown fiercer.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves have nothing to do with each other: one is an Irish wake, the other a comparative adjective. 'Being' is the hinge, and cutting the clue anywhere else leaves both halves meaningless.
explanation.definitionFit: A keener is the professional mourner who keens at a wake; separately, keener is the comparative of keen, meaning sharper or more intense.

clue.text: Van I ran manufactured to produce bliss

indicators.note: something manufactured has been put together out of parts, and letters put together that way end up in an order that is not their own.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, three short words run together

explanation.surface: A driver boasting about the vehicle he once built and drove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van I ran' is built to read as a relative clause rather than a heap of letters, and 'manufactured' sounds like something a van factory does. In Buddhism the state named is the extinction of desire, not merely great happiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Nirvana is used loosely in English for perfect bliss, borrowed from the Buddhist word for release from suffering and rebirth.

parts.note: 'cor' is the British exclamation of amazement — cor blimey — and the spoken equivalent of wow
a group of things that belong together is a set

explanation.surface: A piece of underwear that gets an admiring noise out of a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'wow' are the only sign that a noise is wanted and not a meaning. 'Cor' is a London exclamation of the sort a crossword expects a solver to own outright.
explanation.definitionFit: A corset is the stiffened garment laced round the waist under clothes to shape the body, so it is one particular undergarment.

definitions.note: Trousers is a plural-only noun naming a single article of clothing, so the singular 'garment' is the right word for one pair of them.

indicators.note: 'possibly' says these letters could come out as something other than what they say, and the only thing that can change about a fixed set of letters is their order.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder, the apostrophe carrying no letter of its own

explanation.surface: The kind of clothing somebody who lounges about all day would choose.
explanation.walkthrough: An apostrophe-s reads as possession and is easy to forget as a letter, but it is fodder like everything else. The shuffling signal arrives last, after the eye has stopped looking for one.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the full-length leg garment, a phrase that survives chiefly from the days when boys graduated to them out of shorts.

clue.text: Unworldly one in part of a church

indicators.note: 'in' places whatever stands before it inside whatever comes after, so the short piece is swallowed by the long one.

parts.note: the nave is the long central body of a church, where the congregation sits
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An innocent soul standing somewhere inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is the smallest and most useful piece in cryptic crosswords, standing for I, A or AN as the letters demand. The insertion lands in the middle of a four-letter word, which leaves no seam to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive means innocent of how the world actually works, which is what unworldly says — both adjectives for somebody untouched by experience.

indicators.note: 'in' puts the piece named before it inside the one named after it, so a single letter goes within the longer word.

parts.note: a sash is the broad band worn round the waist
L is the standard abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: Taking some of the length off a band worn at the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' could just as easily be an instruction to remove a letter as the definition, and that choice is what the clue is betting on. The inserted letter lands after the first letter of the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: To slash is to cut with a long sweeping stroke, and the noun does the same job: a slash in a sleeve is a cut in it.

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part instead of the whole, and the part of a phrase that can be lifted out entire is a run of its letters.

parts.note: four letters in a row, running out of the end of the first word and into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A question about how much ground a sea eagle claims as its own.
explanation.walkthrough: An erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a bird whose name survives mostly in crosswords and their hidden runs. The same four words define and conceal at once, so there is no separate definition to hunt for.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the only ground an erne truly holds is the patch it builds on, not the miles of water it hunts over.

indicators.note: letters said to be out are letters out of place, no longer standing where they were put.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the whole word

explanation.surface: A process that strains out whatever is too small to matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filters out' is such a natural phrase that the second word is almost impossible to see as a separate instruction, and that is the whole of the trick. Seven letters with a one-word signal is as bare as an anagram gets.
explanation.definitionFit: Trifles are matters of no importance, so the plural noun answers the plural definition without any adjustment.

parts.note: the head of 'air' is the letter it starts with
the base of a column or a page is its foot

explanation.surface: A modest scatterbrain going about on foot rather than by car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airhead' is one word on the page and two instructions underneath, which is why nothing in the clue looks like a letter-picking signal. 'Humble' is wanted as the verb, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To abase somebody is to humble them, bring them low — both transitive verbs taking the same sort of object.

clue.text: Cosy chat but Jack, perhaps, changed the rota

indicators.note: to change a thing is to leave it not as it was, and the only thing that can change about a fixed set of letters is the order they stand in.

parts.note: a jack in a pack of cards belongs to one of the four suits, and 'perhaps' lets the setter name whichever one suits him
the seven letters of 'the rota' in a different order

explanation.surface: A friendly talk spoiled when somebody called Jack rewrote the duty roster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a man's name because the clue gives him something to do. A rota is the British word for a duty roster, the list saying who works which shift.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart-to-heart is a frank private conversation between two people, which is what a cosy chat becomes once it turns serious.
